- In eighteenth-century Germany and France, executioners collected and sold the blood and fat of the beheaded, and apothecaries gave human fat trade names like "women's butter" and "poor sinner's fat"
- England's Charles II made a tincture of human skull in his private laboratory at Whitehall, with half a pound of opium in the recipe

Many prescriptions worked by **association**: urine for jaundice, essence of hair for baldness, and for a muddled head, a dose of "essence of skull".

Some had a point, by accident: bile dissolves earwax, saliva contains natural antibacterial compounds, and disgusting things make you vomit. More important, bruises, coughs and indigestion clear up by themselves in a few days, and there were no controlled trials. The editor of *The Merck Manual* says 25 to 40 percent of people respond even to sugar pills for pain; not until about 1920 did the average patient seeing the average doctor "benefit on the whole". The remedies often contained alcohol and opium, which cured nothing but at least killed pain and lifted spirits.

points.h: Really just a matter of habit
points.body:
Roach says treating rheumatism with bone marrow or scrofula with sweat is no stranger than treating dwarfism with human growth hormone. We accept transfusions of human blood but wince at the image of steeping in it.

The practice carried into the twentieth century: the Soviet Union transfused **cadaver blood** for 28 years (about 25 tons in all, supplying seventy percent of one clinic's blood), because for six to eight hours after death the blood is sterile and the red cells can still carry oxygen. Dr. Kevorkian tried it in the United States too, but told no one. Some people today still eat their own placentas.

points.h: China: flesh cut for ailing parents, and placenta capsules
points.body:
The scholar Key Ray Chong compiled records, from the Song dynasty to the early twentieth century, of children (mostly daughters-in-law) cutting off their own flesh as medicine for gravely ill elders; the Ming dynasty alone has 286 pieces of thigh flesh, 24 livers and more. Li Shizhen himself disapproved, believing no parent should ask a child for such a sacrifice.

As for reports that Shenzhen hospitals sold aborted fetuses as tonics, Roach had a friend of her interpreter Sandy Wan investigate undercover: direct sales had been banned, but hospitals would prescribe "fetal treasure capsules" made from placentas and aborted embryos. To Roach, the biggest problem was that **the mothers' consent was never sought**.

Reuters reported in 1991 that workers at a crematorium in Hainan cut the buttocks and thighs off bodies for dumplings at a brother's restaurant, and were caught by relatives who came to view a body. Roach flew to Haikou and, with the help of her interpreter Sandy, found the crematorium. The director, a woman about six feet tall, heard her out and fumed for ten minutes: in more than ten years there she had never heard of it, and "it is a disgusting story".

They went on to check at the library: the newspaper cited in the report did not exist, and neither did the restaurant. Roach suspects an urban legend.

Anthropologists say humans have never treated their own kind as everyday food, and the reason is **economics**: omnivores are inefficient at turning calories into meat, so raising people makes less sense than raising cattle. By body composition, human flesh is about the same as veal.

The only group Roach knows of that regularly eats its own kind is California's dogs: euthanized pets are sent to rendering plants and made into bone meal, a common dog food ingredient. As for humans, they won't be turned into fertilizer unless they want to be. That sets up the next chapter.

expressions.en: if you knew where to look and you had a lot of cash and a tote bag you didn't care about
expressions.zh: To buy a mellified man in a twelfth-century Arabian market, you had to know where to look, bring plenty of cash, and have a tote bag you didn't mind ruining.

expressions.en: This is less comforting than it sounds
expressions.zh: Li Shizhen took care to say he wasn't sure the mellified man was real. Roach says that is less reassuring than it sounds, because it means the entries he didn't flag, he believed.

expressions.en: the young carrot-top
expressions.zh: The young redhead. *Carrot-top* is a playful name for a red-haired person.

expressions.en: "its greatest use is for catching fish"
expressions.zh: Louis XIV's apothecary admitted his shop sold mummy, but said its greatest use was as fishing bait.

expressions.en: the cure being worse than the complaint
expressions.zh: A version of *the cure is worse than the disease*.

expressions.en: "very beneficial in flatulency" (which, if he meant as a causative agent, I do not doubt)
expressions.zh: An apothecary claimed mummy was very good for flatulence. Roach's jab: if he meant that it causes it, she doesn't doubt it.

expressions.en: We gave Mrs. Peterson some shit for her quinsy and now she's doing fine!
expressions.zh: Roach's mock testimonial in the style of the period. *Shit* is meant literally here.

expressions.en: I would give my eyeteeth
expressions.zh: *Would give my eyeteeth* means "would give anything for". She adds in parentheses that human eyeteeth were said to cure malaria, breast abscesses and smallpox, so the idiom becomes literal.

expressions.en: It's the sort of defense that might work well for those maladjusted cooks
expressions.zh: Kevorkian dismissed patient objections as "an emotional reaction to a new and slightly unpleasant idea". Roach says the same defense might suit those deranged cooks who play tricks with the pasta sauce.

expressions.en: Do me chicken!
expressions.zh: The English sign of a fried-chicken shop in Haikou, probably aiming for the American *We Do Chicken Right!*. She later uses *Well, do me chicken* as an exclamation.

expressions.en: as tall as the smokestack outside and as likely to belch forth smoke
expressions.zh: The director was as tall as the smokestack outside, and just as liable to blow smoke, that is, to lose her temper.

expressions.en: Unless, I thought to myself, the beach suffers from nightmares, ulcers, ophthalmia, or fetid perspiration.
expressions.zh: A sign on the beach says "No spitting". Roach thinks: unless the beach has nightmares, ulcers, eye inflammation or smelly sweat, all conditions that old saliva cures were meant to treat.

expressions.en: "The little people of the world are hardly worth eating."
expressions.zh: An anthropologist says the malnourished are "hardly worth eating". Roach notes she can only assume he means the malnourished of the Third World, not little people.

questions: Roach says what we eat and won't eat is "mostly a matter of habit". Do you agree? Is there a line you think is more than habit?
The *Compendium of Materia Medica* is highly regarded in China. How did you feel reading the parts of this chapter that quote it?
What view of filial piety does the practice of cutting one's own flesh for a sick parent reflect? Li Shizhen opposed it. What do you think?

lede: Beyond burial and cremation, how else can a person "end"? Roach looks at two new methods: "water resolution", which dissolves the body in lye, and "ecological burial", which freezes and shatters the body and turns it into compost. The real obstacle is not technology but dignity.

points.h: Tissue digestion: a pressure cooker with Drano
points.body:
At Colorado State University's veterinary hospital, dead cows, sheep and horses don't go to a morgue but to a cooler, and then into a stainless steel tank about the size of a hot tub: water plus lye, under pressure and heat for a few hours. What remains is 2 to 3 percent of the body weight, a heap of bone shells that crumble when pinched, and the rest becomes a sterile "coffee-colored" liquid flushed down the drain.

The inventor, Kaye, doesn't dress it up: "In effect, it's a pressure cooker with Drano."
- It destroys prions (mad cow disease), which rendering plants can't
- It emits no pollution
- It costs about a tenth as much as cremation

points.h: The funeral industry is interested: "water resolution"
points.body:
After a Georgia crematorium was found to have 339 uncremated bodies piled up, funeral homes started calling to ask when the machine could be used on people. The funeral consultant McCabe plans to market it like this: "Like cremation, only with pressurized water instead of fire." Roach asks: aren't you leaving out the big part, the lye? He says people will find out, and besides, "watching someone be cremated isn't pretty either".

The bone remains can be ground and scattered, or buried in a small "bone box". As for the body's molecules going down the drain, he says: it's either the sewer or the atmosphere (along with the mercury from dental fillings).

America's first crematorium was built in 1874 by Dr. LeMoyne, an abolitionist who also believed the human body "should never touch water" and went about in a cloud of his own odor. His first customer, Baron de Palm, had already been botched by his embalmers by the time the crematorium was finished; onlookers pulled off the sheet and made crude jokes, and the press complained the ceremony was like a carnival with no religious feeling. Cremation stalled until the Catholic Church relaxed its ban in 1963.

The historian Prothero argues that what funeral reformers really disliked was pomp and extravagance, but they often pushed practicality too far: one proposed tanning human skin into leather, another lighting street lamps with human fat, and Dr. Hay designed a machine to turn bodies into a meat paste and dry it into fertilizer.

Promessa, founded by the Swedish biologist Wiigh-Mäsak, has the support of the Swedish king and the Church of Sweden. The process: the body is immersed in **liquid nitrogen**, shattered into fragments by ultrasound or mechanical vibration, freeze-dried, and placed in a small cornstarch coffin buried shallowly beneath a memorial tree or shrub, where within months it turns to soil.

She is not a practical-minded reformer like Hay but an environmentalist, and Roach says that in parts of Europe environmentalism is close to a religion, so she may well succeed.

She shows off her compost heap the way others show off a new appliance: duck feathers, mussel shells, last week's coleslaw. Her reasoning: people, like ducks, mussels and coleslaw, are part of nature and should go back to the soil after death. To critics who say she reduces the dead to the level of garden waste, she replies:
> Let us raise garden waste to the level of the human body.

She insists that bodies be broken down past recognition before composting: "Can you imagine the family at dinner and someone says, 'Okay, Sven, it's your turn to go out and turn Mother'?"

points.h: The first person to be composted
points.body: In fact, the first person composted was the research subject of an American graduate student, Tim Evans (1998). He wanted to give the poor in rural Haiti and China an alternative to coffins and cremation, and buried a whole donated body in a compost of horse manure and wood shavings, turning it with a rake now and then. Six weeks later it had become "dark, rich soil with good moisture retention", and weeds were growing on top. He said: this is as close to reincarnation as science can get.

Sweden's new emissions rules for crematorium mercury, and the practice of digging up graves after 25 years for reuse, both give compost burial an opening. But the funeral industry worries about its coffin business. At Fonus, the largest funeral company in Scandinavia, an executive asks: is there an ethical problem with shattering a body? She answers that with ultrasound at least no violence is visible, and she hopes families can watch through glass: "I want a method I can show children without them crying." When someone objects that you can't remove the water, which is 70 percent of a person, she says: "The coffee you are drinking has been your neighbor's urine."

After the meeting the executives pose for photos with her and say they'll add a link to Promessa on their website. A cautious friendship has begun.

points.h: Dignity is all in the packaging
points.body:
A monsignor of the American Catholic Church finds composting disrespectful, explaining: "When I was a boy we had a pit where we threw apple peels for fertilizer, and that's what I associate it with." The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency doesn't regulate crematoriums, because if it did, it would have to use the Clean Air Act's provisions on "solid waste incineration", effectively calling the dead solid waste.

Roach's summary: **no method of disposing of a body is truly dignified**. Decay, cremation, dissection, water resolution and composting are all a bit unpleasant, and become acceptable only through carefully chosen euphemisms. She used to think burial at sea was beautiful, until someone told her the cleanest method is to put the body in a tide pool full of Dungeness crabs: "two or three days and it's done." She supports both companies: in life and in death, there should be choices.

expressions.en: A horse, bisected mid-torso, lies in halves on the floor, a vaudeville costume after the show.
expressions.zh: A horse cut in half at the middle lies on the floor like a two-person pantomime horse costume after the show.

expressions.en: "In effect, it's a pressure cooker with Drano,"
expressions.zh: "In effect, it's a pressure cooker with drain cleaner." The inventor's own words; Roach admires him for not prettying it up. Drano is an American brand of drain cleaner.

expressions.en: You don't digest it, it digests you.
expressions.zh: Lye works the same way it would if you swallowed it: you don't digest it, it digests you.

expressions.en: "Just like french fries," says Spracher quietly.
expressions.zh: As the basket of remains is lowered into the tank, the pathologist says quietly: just like french fries.

expressions.en: Gordon Kaye refers to the smell as "soaplike," leading one to wonder where he buys his toiletries.
expressions.zh: The inventor says the smell is "soaplike", which makes you wonder where he buys his toiletries.

expressions.en: traveled about in his own personal miasma
expressions.zh: Dr. LeMoyne believed the body shouldn't touch water, so he went everywhere in "his own personal miasma". The chapter has just explained the period belief that cemeteries gave off miasmas.

expressions.en: like a lasagna baked by an unsupervised child
expressions.zh: Her compost is a jumble of unidentifiable bits, like a lasagna baked by a child left unsupervised.

expressions.en: not so much an explanation as a criminal confession
expressions.zh: Roach says she has no garden, so she doesn't compost; to Wiigh-Mäsak this sounds less like an explanation than a confession of guilt.

expressions.en: Compared to some of the things I've been smelling these days, it's a pot of posies.
expressions.zh: Compared to what I've been smelling lately, this compost is a pot of flowers.

expressions.en: Okay, Sven, it's your turn to go out and turn Mother
expressions.zh: *Turn* means turning a compost heap, and applied to Mother it becomes black comedy.

expressions.en: "The coffee you are drinking has been your neighbor's urine."
expressions.zh: Roach says a woman who can toss the word *urine* into a corporate meeting deserves admiration.

expressions.en: The name hits my ears as Elf Helsing, causing great internal merriment.
expressions.zh: She hears the name Ulf Helsing as "Elf Helsing" and is privately delighted; after that, the executives in matching gray suits become "the elves".

expressions.en: I tell her I'm rooting for her, then quickly rephrase the sentiment, omitting gardening-related verbs.
expressions.zh: *Rooting for* means cheering on, but it also sounds like putting down roots, so she quickly rephrases to avoid gardening verbs.

expressions.en: "very important to feel I'm not crazy."
expressions.zh: Wiigh-Mäsak finally confides that it was, and is, very important to feel she is not crazy. The chapter ends on a sincere note.

questions: Water resolution, composting, cremation, burial, burial at sea: if you could choose, which would you pick? Are your reasons more rational or more emotional?
Roach says dignity is all in the packaging. Are euphemisms necessary, or a form of self-deception?
Wiigh-Mäsak says we should "raise garden waste to the level of the human body". Does that line move you?

lede: After a whole book about cadavers, Roach finally answers the question readers most want to ask: will she donate her own body? The answer lands somewhere unexpected: what happens after death should be decided by the living.

points.h: Wanting to be a teaching skeleton
points.body:
Anatomy professors often donate their own bodies: "I like teaching anatomy, and after I die I can keep teaching." In Renaissance Padua, old professors would ask a favorite student to turn their skull into a specimen. Roach wants to be the skeleton in a medical school classroom: skeletons don't age and look good, unlike an eighty-year-old cadaver that unnerves young students. She also likes the idea of being a mystery to some future medical student: who was this woman?

Then she learns: making a skeleton means stripping the flesh first and boiling the bones for weeks (later done with maggots and carrion beetles instead); no one in the United States makes whole skeletons, they all used to be imported from Calcutta, and in 1985 India banned exports after a scandal over children being abducted and killed for their bones. Her skeleton dream died there.

Next she thinks of donating her brain to the Harvard Brain Bank, for an unserious reason: with a donor card she could say "I'm going to Harvard" and not be lying. A visit changes her mind: frozen brain slices like a chocolate bar, shedding crumbs, and the technician wiping them away says "There goes third grade"; brains are cut in half and stored in ordinary plastic food containers. She had imagined whole brains floating in glass jars, and doesn't want to end up as bits in a freezer storeroom.

points.h: Plastination: preserved for ten thousand years
points.body:
Plastination replaces the water in tissue with a silicone polymer, leaving specimens dry, odorless and unmistakably real. Von Hagens's *Body Worlds* exhibition poses skinned bodies swimming, riding horses and playing chess; eight million people have seen it, and it has drawn the anger of churches and conservatives.

At the University of Michigan, Roach watches bodies dehydrated in acetone, then put in a vacuum chamber to draw in the polymer, and finally posed like clay figures and hardened. A funeral home says commercial plastination costs about $50,000 and lasts at least ten thousand years. On a professor's whiteboard is written "Maria Lopez, brain, for daughter's science fair", and she feels this is what she wants: after death, to visit classrooms and science fairs and spark children's interest in science.

points.h: Controlling what happens after death is fear of not existing
points.body: Roach reflects that elaborately specified arrangements for after death may come from fear of nonexistence: a way to keep exerting influence, to remain "present", after you are gone. The funeral consultant McCabe is blunter: "It's none of their business what happens to them when they die." Directors of body donation programs also tell children who object to their father's donation: make the choice that is best for you; you are the ones who have to live with the decision.

Roach's father, who was not religious, asked to be cremated in a pine coffin with no memorial service. Her Catholic mother complied but came to regret it: people in town complained to her face about the lack of a service, the Church required that ashes be buried, and she didn't want them in the house. The urn sat in a closet for a year or two, and then, without telling the children, she buried it beside the plot she had reserved for herself. Roach at first sided with her father, but later understood how much pain those wishes had caused her mother and changed her mind.

Her husband Ed can't even wear contact lenses, because he would have to touch his eyes. If she donated her body, he would have to picture her on a dissecting table. So her decision:
- **Ed can do whatever he wants**
- The one exception is organ donation: if she is brain-dead and her organs are usable, "squeamish or not, someone needs them"
- If Ed dies first, she will fill out the body donation form

She will attach a short self-introduction to her file (this is allowed), so the student who dissects her can look down at her worn-out hull and say, "Hey, look, I got the woman who wrote the book about cadavers." Her last line: if there's any way to arrange it, **I'll make the thing wink.**

expressions.en: I've enjoyed hanging around in rooms doing nothing much, and look, I get to do it after I die.
expressions.zh: A riff on the professor's "I like teaching anatomy, and after I die I can keep teaching": I've always liked hanging around in rooms doing nothing, and after I die I can keep at it. For a skeleton, *hang around* is also literal.

expressions.en: People really need to think these requests through.
expressions.zh: A Shakespearean actor willed his skull to his theater company to play Yorick (the skull in *Hamlet*). Thinking of the weeks of boiling required first, Roach says people really should think such requests through.

expressions.en: dogs small enough to fit into bicycle baskets
expressions.zh: Animals don't get diagnosable mental illness, though cats and "dogs small enough to fit into bicycle baskets" seem to come with their own psychological problems.

expressions.en: You do not need brains to go to the Harvard Brain Bank, only a brain.
expressions.zh: You don't need to be smart (*brains*) to go to the Harvard Brain Bank, just to have *a brain*. A pun on the plural and singular.

expressions.en: It sliced as does a Butterfinger, with little shards crumbling off.
expressions.zh: Frozen brain cuts like a Butterfinger candy bar, with crumbs falling off.

expressions.en: "There goes third grade."
expressions.zh: The technician's remark as he wipes away brain crumbs. He promptly gets into trouble for this sort of comment.

expressions.en: If not glass, at least Tupperware. I wondered what the dorms look like these days.
expressions.zh: Brains in ordinary food containers. Roach expected more of Harvard: if not glass, at least Tupperware. She wonders what the dorms look like these days.

expressions.en: making brain harvesting sound like something that takes just minutes and wipes clean with a damp cloth
expressions.zh: A spokesperson describes brain harvesting in the breezy tone of a TV infomercial host, as if it took minutes and wiped clean with a damp cloth.

expressions.en: about as eternal as anyone in their right, or even their wrong, mind could care about
expressions.zh: Ten thousand years is about the limit of eternity that anyone in their right mind, or even their wrong one, could care about.

expressions.en: "It's none of their business what happens to them when they die,"
expressions.zh: The funeral consultant's line, which is also the chapter's turning point: what happens to people after death is not their business.

expressions.en: "Ix-nay on the ainbank-bray."
expressions.zh: Her husband says "No brain bank talk" in Pig Latin, a children's word game: *ix-nay* is *nix*, *ainbank-bray* is *brainbank*.

expressions.en: my dilapidated hull
expressions.zh: My worn-out shell. *Hull* calls back to the word Roach used for her mother's body in the introduction, bookending the book.

expressions.en: And if there's any way I can arrange it, I'll make the thing wink.
expressions.zh: If there's a way to arrange it, I'll make it wink. The book's last line closes by putting humor and death side by side.

questions: In the end Roach leaves the decision to her husband. Do you agree that what happens after death should be decided by the living?
She says wanting to control what happens after death comes from fear of not existing. What do you think about what should happen to you after you die?
Having read the whole book, have your views of death and dead bodies changed? Which chapter affected you most?
